definition: involving a great deal of effort, trouble, or difficulty

examples.text: Peasants owed their lords onerous duties, including weeks of unpaid labor each year.
Recording the temperature by hand every hour was an onerous task before sensors existed.
Filling out six scholarship forms in one weekend felt onerous, but it paid off.

confused.note: Onerous means burdensome; ominous means threatening.

questions.passage: Small farms complained that the new reporting rules were ______. Each week they had to log every animal's feed, weight, and medication by hand, a job that took one worker nearly two full days.
questions.explanation: A weekly job that takes two days of labor is a heavy burden.

distractors.why: Trivial means of little importance or effort, the opposite of two days of work.
Ambiguous means unclear; the rules are clear but demanding.
Clandestine means secret, which does not describe official reporting rules.

definition: so ordinary and unoriginal that it is boring

examples.text: The reviewer dismissed the novel's banal plot as a copy of a hundred earlier romances.
The diplomat's speech was a string of banal remarks about friendship between nations.
The greeting card's banal message could have been written for anyone.

confused.note: Mundane means everyday and routine; banal is a sharper criticism meaning boringly unoriginal.

questions.passage: The film's visuals are stunning, but its dialogue is ______. Characters announce that "love conquers all" and that "you must follow your heart," lines audiences have heard countless times before.
questions.explanation: Lines heard countless times before are unoriginal and dull.

distractors.why: Cryptic means puzzling and hard to interpret, but these lines are all too familiar.
Eloquent means movingly expressive, which the critic denies.
Ornate means elaborately decorated; these lines are plain clichés.

definition: an award or expression of praise

examples.text: The Nobel Prize was the final accolade in the physicist's long career.
Her first novel won every major accolade, which made writing the second one terrifying.
Being named team captain was the accolade my brother wanted most.

confused.note: An accolade is an honor; an accord is an agreement.

questions.passage: The restaurant has received many ______ since it opened, including a national award for its desserts and a place on three critics' lists of the year's best new kitchens.
questions.explanation: Awards and places on best-of lists are honors.

distractors.why: Discrepancies are mismatches between things that should agree, not honors.
Rebukes are sharp criticisms, the opposite of awards.
Anomalies are departures from the norm, which does not describe awards.

definition: the quality of being open and honest

examples.text: The general's candor about the army's losses shocked a public used to cheerful reports.
The memoir is admired for its candor about the author's failures as a parent.
I appreciated my friend's candor when she told me the haircut was a mistake.

confused.note: Candor is the noun; candid is the adjective.

questions.passage: Company reports usually bury bad news in footnotes. This one is notable for its ______: the first page states plainly that sales fell by a third and that management's own forecast was wrong.
questions.explanation: Stating bad news plainly on page one shows openness and honesty.

distractors.why: Duplicity means deceitfulness, the opposite of admitting errors openly.
Brevity means shortness; the report is praised for honesty, not length.
Alacrity means eager readiness, which does not describe a report.

definition: to make someone less angry, often by giving them something they want

examples.text: The king lowered the grain tax to placate the rioting townspeople.
The hero offers a gift of honey to placate the dragon.
The airline tried to placate delayed passengers with meal vouchers.

confused.note: Placate is a verb meaning to calm someone; placid is an adjective meaning calm.

questions.passage: When fans learned that the concert had been cancelled an hour before it was to start, many were furious. The organizers sought to ______ them by offering full refunds and free tickets to a future show.
questions.explanation: Refunds and free tickets were meant to calm angry fans.

distractors.why: Antagonize means to make hostile, the opposite of the organizers' aim.
Deride means to mock, which would anger fans further.
Emulate means to imitate, which does not fit the situation.

definition: enjoying the company of other people; sociable

examples.text: Starlings are gregarious birds that roost in flocks of many thousands.
The gregarious aunt fills the quiet house with guests within a day of her arrival.
My gregarious roommate had met everyone on our floor before I finished unpacking.

confused.note: Gregarious means sociable; egregious means shockingly bad.

questions.passage: Unlike her twin, who preferred to read alone, Dalia was ______. She joined four clubs in her first month at college and was rarely seen eating a meal without a crowd of friends.
questions.explanation: Joining clubs and always eating with friends shows she loves company.

distractors.why: Reclusive means avoiding people, which describes her twin more than her.
Diligent means hardworking; the passage is about sociability.
Egregious means outrageously bad, a look-alike word with an unrelated meaning.

definition: friendly and easy to talk to

examples.text: The affable president chatted with reporters as if they were old neighbors.
The villain hides his plans behind an affable smile.
Our affable mail carrier always stops to pet the dog.

confused.note: Both mean friendly; affable stresses being easy to approach and talk with.

questions.passage: Students expecting a stern lecture from the visiting judge were pleasantly surprised. She turned out to be ______, joking about her own early mistakes and staying an extra hour to answer questions.
questions.explanation: Joking and lingering to chat show she is friendly and approachable.

distractors.why: Brusque means abrupt and curt, which students feared but did not find.
Pedantic means fussy about minor points of learning, which the passage does not show.
Reticent means reluctant to speak, but she talked freely.

definition: to praise something or someone very highly

examples.text: Pamphlets extolled the fertile land of the West to attract settlers.
The poem extols the courage of ordinary sailors.
My dad extols the virtues of waking up at five, but nobody else is convinced.

confused.note: Extol means to praise highly; extort means to get something by threats.

questions.passage: Travel writers of the 1920s ______ the new highway, calling it "a ribbon of wonder" and urging every reader to drive its length at least once.
questions.explanation: Glowing descriptions and urging readers to go are high praise.

distractors.why: Disparaged means belittled, the opposite of this praise.
Scrutinized means examined closely; the writers were praising, not inspecting.
Rescinded means officially cancelled, which makes no sense for writers and a highway.

definition: showing great care, attention, and steady effort

examples.text: Through assiduous observation, she recorded the nesting habits of a single owl family for nine years.
The assiduous scribe checked each copy of the law against the original.
He was assiduous about watering the seedlings and never missed a morning.

confused.note: Assiduous means hardworking and careful; acidulous means sharp or sour in tone.

questions.passage: The discovery owed less to luck than to ______ effort. For eleven years the astronomer photographed the same patch of sky every clear night, comparing each new image with the last.
questions.explanation: Photographing the sky every clear night for eleven years is steady, careful work.

distractors.why: Sporadic means occasional and irregular, the opposite of nightly effort.
Cursory means hasty and shallow, which this work was not.
Fortuitous means happening by chance, which the first sentence rules out.

definition: having no clear shape, form, or structure

examples.text: Glass is an amorphous solid, lacking the ordered pattern of a crystal.
The ghost appears as an amorphous gray shape at the foot of the stairs.
Our plans for the summer were still amorphous in June.

confused.note: Amorphous means shapeless; amorous means showing romantic love.

questions.passage: In its first draft the proposal was ______, a loose collection of hopes with no budget, timeline, or list of tasks. Only after weeks of revision did it take on a definite structure.
questions.explanation: A plan with no budget, timeline, or tasks has no clear structure.

distractors.why: Meticulous means carefully detailed, the opposite of the first draft.
Cogent means clear and convincing, which a loose set of hopes is not.
Onerous means burdensome, which does not describe a vague draft.

definition: possible to do or achieve

examples.text: With current batteries, a solar-powered flight across the ocean is barely feasible.
A canal across the isthmus became feasible only after engineers controlled the fever.
Biking to school is feasible in September but not in a January blizzard.

confused.note: Feasible means it can be done; plausible means it can be believed.

questions.passage: Engineers agreed that a tunnel under the bay would be the ideal solution. The question was whether it was ______: the seabed was soft mud, and no machine then available could bore through it safely.
questions.explanation: The doubt is whether the tunnel can actually be built.

distractors.why: Plausible means believable; the issue is whether the tunnel can be built, not believed.
Superfluous means unnecessary, but the tunnel is called the ideal solution.
Arbitrary means based on whim, which does not fit an engineering question.

definition: to slow down or prevent a process or action

examples.text: Cold temperatures inhibit the growth of most bacteria.
Heavy tariffs inhibited trade between the neighboring states.
Fear of looking foolish inhibits many students from asking questions.

confused.note: Inhibit means to hold back; inhabit means to live in.

questions.passage: Gardeners often spread a layer of bark around young trees. The bark blocks sunlight from reaching the soil and thus ______ the growth of weeds that would otherwise compete for water.
questions.explanation: Blocking sunlight holds back weed growth.

distractors.why: Facilitates means makes easier, the opposite of blocking sunlight.
Emulates means imitates, which does not fit bark and weeds.
Extols means praises highly, which makes no sense for bark.

definition: calm, quiet, and peaceful

examples.text: The story begins in a tranquil village where nothing has happened for a hundred years.
The lake's tranquil surface hid strong currents below.
Early morning is the only tranquil time in a house with three dogs.

confused.note: Tranquil is the adjective meaning calm; to tranquilize is to calm with a drug.

questions.passage: After a week of honking traffic and crowded sidewalks, the travelers found the mountain monastery wonderfully ______. The only sounds were wind in the pines and, at dusk, a single bell.
questions.explanation: Wind, pines, and one bell describe a calm, quiet place.

distractors.why: Turbulent means wild and unsettled, which describes the city they left.
Austere means severely plain; the sentence stresses quiet, not plainness.
Ominous means threatening, the wrong tone for a place found "wonderfully" calm.

definition: quiet, modest, and reserved in manner

examples.text: The heroine's demure manner hides a sharp wit and a stubborn will.
Portraits of the era show young women in demure poses, eyes lowered.
My usually loud cousin was oddly demure when she met her favorite singer.

confused.note: Demure is an adjective meaning modest; demur is a verb meaning to object mildly.

questions.passage: On stage the comedian is loud and outrageous. Offstage, friends say, she is surprisingly ______, speaking softly, dressing plainly, and blushing when strangers recognize her.
questions.explanation: Soft speech, plain dress, and blushing show a modest, reserved manner.

distractors.why: Flamboyant means showy, which describes her stage persona.
Belligerent means hostile, which the passage does not suggest.
Gregarious means sociable; someone who blushes when recognized is reserved.

definition: done quietly and secretly to avoid being noticed

examples.text: The boy casts a furtive look at the door before opening the forbidden book.
Smugglers made furtive landings along the coast on moonless nights.
She took a furtive bite of the cake before the guests arrived.

confused.note: Furtive means sneaky; a fugitive is a person who is running away.

questions.passage: The examiner noticed that one student kept making ______ glances at the cuff of his sleeve, looking down quickly whenever her back was turned and straightening up the moment she faced him.
questions.explanation: Glances made only when her back is turned are sneaky and secret.

distractors.why: Candid means open and honest, the opposite of this behavior.
Benign means harmless, which does not describe suspicious glances.
Languid means slow and relaxed, but these glances were quick.

definition: having or showing very strong and sincere feeling

examples.text: Fervent supporters walked for days to hear the candidate speak.
The letter ends with a fervent plea for forgiveness.
My sister is a fervent believer that pineapple belongs on pizza.

confused.note: Fervent and fervid both mean passionate; fervid often suggests feeling that is too heated.

questions.passage: The naturalist was a ______ defender of wetlands. She wrote hundreds of letters to lawmakers, spoke at every public hearing, and once stood in a marsh for six hours to block a bulldozer.
questions.explanation: Hundreds of letters and blocking a bulldozer show intense, sincere commitment.

distractors.why: Apathetic means uncaring, the opposite of her efforts.
Furtive means sneaky, but her defense was loud and public.
Tentative means hesitant, which does not describe her bold actions.

definition: worried or afraid that something bad may happen

examples.text: The narrator grows apprehensive as the train nears the town he fled years ago.
Farmers were apprehensive about the new railway cutting through their fields.
I was apprehensive about the first day at a new school, but it went fine.

confused.note: Apprehensive means worried; comprehensive means complete and wide-ranging.

questions.passage: Although the surgeon had performed the operation hundreds of times, the patient remained ______, asking twice more about the risks and gripping the arms of her chair as she waited.
questions.explanation: Repeated questions about risks and a tight grip show worry.

distractors.why: Complacent means untroubled and self-satisfied, the opposite of her state.
Indifferent means not caring, but she clearly cared a great deal.
Jubilant means joyful, which does not fit a nervous patient.

definition: used in ordinary conversation, not in formal speech or writing

examples.text: Twain's colloquial style made his characters sound like real people on the river.
The diary is written in colloquial German, full of slang from the Berlin streets.
"Gonna" is fine in a text but too colloquial for a college essay.

confused.note: Colloquial means conversational; a colloquium is an academic conference.

questions.passage: The translator faced a choice. The original novel is narrated by a teenager in ______ language, full of slang and half-finished sentences, and a formal English version would have lost the narrator's voice entirely.
questions.explanation: Slang and half-finished sentences are features of informal, conversational language.

distractors.why: Lofty means elevated and grand, the kind of style the translator feared would lose the voice.
Arcane means known to few, but slang is everyday speech.
Eloquent means polished and moving, which half-finished sentences are not.

definition: strong, healthy, and unlikely to fail

examples.text: The finding is robust: five independent teams have reproduced it.
A robust trade in salt made the desert city wealthy.
You need a robust umbrella in this wind, not the cheap folding kind.

confused.note: Robust means strong and healthy; rotund means round and plump.

questions.passage: Critics had predicted that the small bookshop could not survive the arrival of online retailers. Twenty years later, its sales are ______, and it has opened two more branches.
questions.explanation: Surviving and expanding show strong, healthy sales.

distractors.why: Tenuous means weak or shaky, which is what critics predicted.
Negligible means too small to matter, which contradicts opening new branches.
Furtive means secretive, which does not describe sales.

definition: false or fake, though seeming to be real or true

examples.text: The apparent link between the two diseases turned out to be spurious.
The pretender backed his claim to the throne with a spurious family tree.
The email offered a spurious prize to anyone who sent their bank details.

confused.note: Spurious means not genuine; specious means sounding right but actually wrong.

questions.passage: The letter was long believed to be the work of the queen herself. Analysis of its ink, which contains a dye not invented until two centuries after her death, has shown the document to be ______.
questions.explanation: Ink from two centuries later proves the letter is a fake.

distractors.why: Authentic means genuine, which the ink evidence disproves.
Ambiguous means open to more than one meaning; the evidence is decisive.
Obsolete means outdated, which is not the same as forged.

definition: done as a routine duty, with little effort, interest, or care

examples.text: He gives his wife a perfunctory kiss and returns to his newspaper.
The guards made a perfunctory search of the wagon and waved it through.
The waiter's perfunctory "How is everything?" came as he was already walking away.

confused.note: Perfunctory means done carelessly as a routine; peremptory means commanding, leaving no room for refusal.

questions.passage: The audience had hoped the author would speak about her new book with some enthusiasm. Instead she gave a ______ ten-minute talk, reading from notes in a flat voice and leaving without taking questions.
questions.explanation: A flat, brief reading with no questions shows minimal effort and interest.

distractors.why: Fervent means passionate, which is what the audience hoped for.
Meticulous means extremely careful, which a hurried talk is not.
Belligerent means aggressive; her talk was lifeless, not hostile.

partsNote: from Latin fungi, "to perform": just getting through it

definition: to see, recognize, or understand something that is not obvious

examples.text: Astronomers can discern a planet by the faint wobble it causes in its star.
Only the old servant discerns the sadness behind the bride's smile.
In the fog I could barely discern the outline of the bridge.

confused.note: To discern is to perceive; discreet means careful not to attract attention.

questions.passage: To an untrained eye the two fossil teeth look the same. A specialist, however, can ______ tiny ridges on one of them that mark it as belonging to a meat eater.
questions.explanation: The specialist can perceive details that others cannot see.

distractors.why: Overlook means to miss, which is what the untrained eye does.
Fabricate means to invent falsely; the specialist finds real ridges.
Disseminate means to spread widely, which does not fit seeing a detail.

definition: playful, fanciful, and a little odd in an appealing way

examples.text: The book's whimsical drawings show hedgehogs in top hats rowing a teacup.
The duke's whimsical garden included a maze shaped like his own signature.
She wears whimsical socks, one with cats and one with pizza slices.

confused.note: Whimsical is usually charming; capricious suggests unpredictable changes that cause trouble.

questions.passage: The architect is known for ______ touches. Her otherwise ordinary library has a reading nook shaped like a whale's mouth and a staircase whose railing ends in the tail of a brass fox.
questions.explanation: A whale-mouth nook and a fox-tail railing are playful and fanciful.

distractors.why: Austere means severely plain, the opposite of playful decoration.
Ominous means threatening, the wrong tone for charming details.
Perfunctory means done without care or interest, which these inventive touches are not.

definition: truthfulness or accuracy

examples.text: Scholars doubt the veracity of the explorer's claim to have reached the pole.
The journal checks the veracity of data before it publishes any study.
My mom questioned the veracity of my story about the homework-eating printer.

confused.note: Veracity means truthfulness; voracity means great hunger or eagerness.

questions.passage: Because the memoir was written forty years after the events it describes, historians were cautious about its ______. They accepted its account only after finding letters from the period that confirmed the key details.
questions.explanation: Historians were unsure whether the memoir was truthful until letters confirmed it.

distractors.why: Brevity means shortness, which is not what the letters confirmed.
Voracity means greediness or great appetite; it only looks like the right word.
Levity means lightheartedness, which is not what historians doubted.

definition: to lecture or criticize someone in a long, loud, and forceful way

examples.text: The general harangued his retreating troops from the back of a wagon.
Every Sunday the aunt harangues the children about the laziness of modern youth.
The coach harangued us for ten minutes about leaving cones on the field.

confused.note: To harangue is to lecture loudly at length; to harass is to bother repeatedly.

questions.passage: Residents had hoped the meeting would be a calm exchange of views. Instead, one council member spent forty minutes ______ the audience, shouting that anyone who opposed the new stadium was an enemy of progress.
questions.explanation: Forty minutes of shouting at an audience is a long, forceful lecture.

distractors.why: Placating means calming, the opposite of shouting accusations.
Extolling means praising highly, but he called opponents enemies.
Emulating means imitating, which does not fit.

definition: to confirm that something is true, correct, or acceptable

examples.text: A second trial validated the vaccine's safety in older adults.
The discovery of the sunken fleet validated the old chronicle's account.
The parking attendant validated our ticket so we could leave without paying.

confused.note: Valid is the adjective; validate is the verb meaning to show that something is valid.

questions.passage: The computer model predicted that the bridge would sway less than two centimeters in high wind. Sensors installed during last winter's storms ______ that prediction, recording a maximum sway of 1.7 centimeters.
questions.explanation: Real measurements matched the prediction, confirming it.

distractors.why: Refuted means disproved, but the measurements agreed with the model.
Exacerbated means made worse, which does not apply to a prediction.
Solicited means asked for; sensors cannot ask for a prediction.

definition: common or widespread at a particular time or in a particular place

examples.text: The disease is most prevalent in regions with standing water.
Belief in witchcraft was prevalent in the villages of that century.
Hoodies are so prevalent at my school that they are practically a uniform.

confused.note: Prevalent means widespread; prevailing means dominant at the moment, as in "prevailing winds" or "prevailing opinion."

questions.passage: Surveys from the 1950s show that the view was ______ among physicians: nearly nine in ten of those questioned believed that ulcers were caused chiefly by stress.
questions.explanation: A belief held by nine in ten physicians was widespread.

distractors.why: Obsolete means no longer in use, but the survey shows the view was widely held then.
Spurious means false; the sentence after the colon is about how many held the view.
Sporadic means scattered and occasional, the opposite of nine in ten.

definition: to make something weaker or less effective, often gradually

examples.text: Several pages of missing data undermined the study's main conclusion.
Rumors of bribery undermined public trust in the court.
Constant interruptions undermined my efforts to finish the essay.

confused.note: Undermine means to weaken; underline means to emphasize.

questions.passage: The lawyer's argument depended on her client having been at home all evening. A parking ticket issued across town at 9 p.m. seriously ______ that claim.
questions.explanation: The ticket weakens the claim that the client stayed home.

distractors.why: Bolstered means strengthened, but the ticket conflicts with the claim.
Disseminated means spread widely, which a parking ticket does not do to a claim.
Placated means calmed someone's anger, which does not fit.

definition: to examine something very carefully

examples.text: Reviewers scrutinized the methods section for any sign of bias.
Customs officers scrutinized every crate that came off the ship.
My dad scrutinizes the restaurant bill as if he were grading an exam.

confused.note: Scrutiny is the noun; scrutinize is the verb.

questions.passage: Before the museum pays for a painting, its experts ______ the work for days, studying the canvas under ultraviolet light, testing the paint, and tracing the record of every previous owner.
questions.explanation: Days of testing and tracing describe very careful examination.

distractors.why: Overlook means to fail to notice, the opposite of days of study.
Embellish means to decorate or exaggerate, which experts would not do to a painting they are checking.
Extol means to praise; the experts are examining, not praising.

definition: to make two different ideas, facts, or people agree or become friendly again

examples.text: The treaty reconciled two kingdoms that had fought for a generation.
Physicists have struggled to reconcile gravity with quantum theory.
I could not reconcile the kind note with the cold way she spoke to me.

confused.note: Reconcile means to bring into agreement; recognize means to identify.

questions.passage: The two eyewitness accounts seem to conflict: one places the fire's start at midnight, the other at dawn. The historian attempts to ______ them by proposing that there were two separate fires.
questions.explanation: Proposing two fires makes the conflicting accounts agree.

distractors.why: Undermine means to weaken, but the historian is trying to save both accounts.
Scrutinize means to examine closely; the proposal goes further and resolves the conflict.
Harangue means to lecture loudly, which makes no sense with accounts.

definition: to draw out a response, answer, or reaction

examples.text: A mild electric pulse elicits a twitch in the muscle.
The detective's casual question elicits an unexpected confession.
My joke elicited groans from the whole table.

confused.note: Elicit is a verb meaning to draw out; illicit is an adjective meaning illegal.

questions.passage: Good interviewers know that yes-or-no questions tend to produce short answers. To ______ longer, more thoughtful responses from a guest, they ask questions that begin with "how" or "why."
questions.explanation: The right questions draw out fuller responses.

distractors.why: Stifle means to hold back, the opposite of the interviewer's goal.
Refute means to disprove, which is not what a question does to an answer.
Illicit is an adjective meaning illegal; it only sounds like the verb needed here.

definition: strange because it does not fit with its surroundings or with what is expected

examples.text: The butler's cheerful whistle seems incongruous in the gloomy mansion.
A Roman column stood incongruous among the market's wooden stalls.
His flip-flops looked incongruous with the suit and tie.

confused.note: The two overlap; incongruous is the usual word for something that seems out of place.

questions.passage: Visitors to the medieval cathedral are often startled by one ______ detail: among the carved saints above the door, a twentieth-century restorer added a small stone astronaut.
questions.explanation: An astronaut among medieval saints does not fit its surroundings.

distractors.why: Conventional means usual and expected, the opposite of this surprise.
Ominous means threatening, which a small stone astronaut is not.
Tranquil means calm, which does not describe a startling detail.

definition: unclear because it can be understood in more than one way, sometimes on purpose

examples.text: The test results were equivocal, so the doctor ordered a second scan.
The oracle's equivocal answer let both kings believe they would win.
When I asked if she liked the gift, her equivocal "It's interesting" told me nothing.

confused.note: Equivocal means unclear or evasive; equitable means fair.

questions.passage: Asked whether she would run for a second term, the governor gave an ______ reply. She said that she "loved the job" but also that "every season comes to an end," leaving reporters unsure what she meant.
questions.explanation: A reply that points both ways and leaves listeners unsure is ambiguous.

distractors.why: Emphatic means forceful and clear, which this reply was not.
Candid means frank and open, but she avoided a direct answer.
Belligerent means hostile, which does not describe her remarks.

definition: to estimate something unknown by extending what is already known

examples.text: From ten years of data, the team extrapolated the glacier's size in 2050.
Historians extrapolate the city's population from the number of bread ovens.
You cannot extrapolate a whole season from one good game.

confused.note: To extrapolate is to extend beyond the known data; to interpolate is to estimate a value between known points.

questions.passage: The survey covered only two hundred households in a single city. Critics warned that it would be risky to ______ from so small a sample to the habits of an entire nation.
questions.explanation: Applying a small sample's results to a whole nation extends beyond the data.

distractors.why: Digress means to wander off the topic, which is not the risk described.
Abstain means to hold back from doing something, which does not fit "from so small a sample to the habits of a nation."
Capitulate means to surrender, which makes no sense here.

definition: so interesting or convincing that it holds your attention or belief

examples.text: The novel's compelling first chapter makes it impossible to stop reading.
The fossils offer compelling evidence that the species lived in herds.
She made a compelling case for adopting the older dog.

confused.note: Compelling means powerfully convincing or interesting; compulsory means required.

questions.passage: Jurors later said the fingerprint evidence was interesting but hardly decisive. What they found truly ______ was the security footage, which showed the defendant entering the building minutes before the alarm sounded.
questions.explanation: Footage that settled the jurors' minds was powerfully convincing.

distractors.why: Tenuous means weak, but this evidence persuaded them.
Superfluous means unnecessary, yet the footage was what decided the case.
Equivocal means unclear, which the footage was not.

definition: doubting that something is true or useful

examples.text: Reviewers were skeptical of results that no other lab had repeated.
Skeptical investors refused to fund the first transatlantic cable.
I was skeptical that a five-minute workout could do anything, and I was right.

confused.note: A skeptical person doubts claims until shown evidence; a cynical person assumes people act from selfish motives.

questions.passage: The company announced that its battery could power a car for a thousand miles on one charge. Engineers elsewhere were ______, noting that the firm had released no test data and had made similar announcements before.
questions.explanation: Pointing to missing data and past announcements shows doubt.

distractors.why: Credulous means too ready to believe, the opposite of their reaction.
Jubilant means joyful, which does not fit engineers raising doubts.
Apathetic means not caring; these engineers cared enough to look for the data.

definition: famous and respected, especially in a profession

examples.text: The eminent chemist had trained half the department's professors.
Several eminent jurists signed the letter protesting the new law.
Our small town's most eminent resident is a retired astronaut.

confused.note: Eminent means distinguished; imminent means about to happen. Immanent means present within.

questions.passage: The conference organizers were thrilled when Dr. Achebe agreed to speak. As one of the most ______ scholars in her field, with four major prizes and a textbook used on six continents, she was certain to draw a crowd.
questions.explanation: Major prizes and a widely used textbook mark her as famous and respected.

distractors.why: Obscure means little known, the opposite of a prizewinning scholar.
Imminent means about to happen; it is a look-alike that cannot describe a person's reputation.
Reticent means reluctant to speak, which is not why she would draw a crowd.

definition: very weak, thin, or uncertain

examples.text: The link between the mineral and better sleep is tenuous at best.
The rebels kept a tenuous hold on the mountain pass through the winter.
My connection to the celebrity is tenuous: my cousin once fixed her car.

confused.note: Tenuous means weak or thin; tenacious means holding on firmly.

questions.passage: The article claims that the two painters influenced each other. The evidence for this is ______, however: they lived in the same city for one year and are not known ever to have met.
questions.explanation: One shared year and no known meeting is weak evidence.

distractors.why: Compelling means convincing, but the evidence is thin.
Tenacious means stubbornly persistent; it resembles the right word but means nearly the reverse.
Copious means abundant, yet the evidence is scant.

definition: following what is usual, traditional, or widely accepted

examples.text: The new drug works faster than conventional treatments.
The novel abandons conventional chapters for a series of letters and receipts.
We skipped the conventional wedding cake and served pie.

confused.note: Conventional means usual or traditional; convenient means easy or handy.

questions.passage: Most cookbooks of the period followed a ______ format, listing ingredients and then steps. Fisher's book broke with that pattern, wrapping each recipe inside a personal essay about the meal where she first tasted the dish.
questions.explanation: A format most cookbooks followed is the usual, traditional one.

distractors.why: Whimsical means playful and odd, which would not describe the standard format.
Incongruous means out of place, but this format was the norm.
Spurious means fake, which does not describe a format.

definition: an unfair preference for or against a person, group, or idea

examples.text: Random assignment guards against bias in choosing who receives the treatment.
The chronicler's bias toward his own king colors every page.
I admit a bias: I think my own dog is the best one at the park.

confused.note: Bias is a leaning that may be mild or unconscious; prejudice is a stronger, fixed judgment made in advance.

questions.passage: To keep judges from favoring musicians they knew, the orchestra began holding auditions behind a screen. The change was designed to remove ______ from the hiring process.
questions.explanation: Favoring known musicians is an unfair preference, which the screen removes.

distractors.why: Candor means honesty, which the orchestra would not want to remove.
Consensus means agreement, which is not the problem being solved.
Brevity means shortness, which is unrelated to favoritism.

definition: present from birth; not learned

examples.text: Newborn turtles have an innate drive to crawl toward the sea.
The heroine's innate sense of fairness sets her against her own family.
My sister has an innate sense of direction; I get lost in parking garages.

confused.note: Innate means present from birth in a living thing; inherent means built into the nature of anything.

questions.passage: Researchers wondered whether the songbird's melody was learned or ______. When chicks raised in silence still produced a rough version of the tune, the team concluded that at least part of it is present from birth.
questions.explanation: A song produced without ever hearing it must be inborn.

distractors.why: Acquired means gained through experience, the alternative the experiment ruled out.
Arbitrary means random, which is not the contrast with "learned."
Ephemeral means short-lived, which is not at issue.

definition: too bold in taking liberties or assuming something without permission

examples.text: The duke finds it presumptuous of the tutor to offer advice on matters of state.
Critics called it presumptuous for a new nation to lecture older ones.
It felt presumptuous to call my teacher by her first name, so I asked first.

confused.note: Presumptuous means overstepping; presumptive means assumed to be the case, as in "the presumptive winner."

questions.passage: The intern had been at the firm for only three days. Senior partners therefore thought it ______ of him to rearrange the conference room and announce that, from now on, meetings would follow his agenda.
questions.explanation: A newcomer taking charge without permission is overstepping.

distractors.why: Deferential means respectfully yielding, the opposite of his behavior.
Diffident means shy and unsure, which he clearly was not.
Prudent means wise and careful, which the partners did not think.

definition: bad-tempered and sulky in a childish way

examples.text: The petulant prince throws his spoon across the hall when dessert is late.
The minister's petulant letters complain that nobody appreciates his genius.
I got petulant when my sister beat me at chess three times in a row.

confused.note: Petulant means sulky; pestilent means harmful or troublesome, like a plague.

questions.passage: When the referee ruled against him, the star player did not argue the point calmly. He gave a ______ shrug, kicked the ball into the stands, and refused to speak to his teammates for the rest of the half.
questions.explanation: Kicking the ball away and refusing to speak is childish sulking.

distractors.why: Magnanimous means generous and forgiving, the opposite of his reaction.
Stoic means enduring without complaint, which he did not do.
Judicious means showing good judgment, which this outburst lacked.

definition: stubbornly refusing to obey rules or orders

examples.text: The governor sent troops to deal with the recalcitrant province.
The recalcitrant bacteria resisted every antibiotic the lab tried.
Our recalcitrant printer ignores every command until someone hits it.

confused.note: Recalcitrant means actively defiant; reluctant means merely unwilling.

questions.passage: Most of the town's shop owners accepted the new signage rules without complaint. A few ______ merchants, however, kept their old neon signs lit even after receiving three written warnings and a fine.
questions.explanation: Ignoring warnings and a fine is stubborn refusal to obey.

distractors.why: Compliant means obedient, which describes the other shop owners.
Affable means friendly, which is unrelated to refusing the rules.
Apprehensive means worried; merchants who ignored a fine showed no fear.

definition: much higher than is reasonable, especially of a price

examples.text: Grain merchants charged exorbitant prices during the famine.
The exorbitant cost of the telescope forced three countries to share it.
The stadium charges an exorbitant nine dollars for a bottle of water.

confused.note: Exorbitant describes a price or demand that is far too high; extravagant describes spending or behavior that goes beyond reasonable limits.

questions.passage: Collectors were once willing to pay ______ sums for the rare stamp, with one example selling for more than the price of a house. Since a large hoard was discovered in 2019, prices have fallen to a fraction of that.
questions.explanation: More than the price of a house for a stamp is far beyond reasonable.

distractors.why: Negligible means too small to matter, the opposite of a house-sized sum.
Tenuous means weak or thin, which does not describe a price.
Prevalent means widespread, which is not what a sum of money can be.

definition: refusing to change one's position or to compromise

examples.text: Both sides were intransigent, and the strike dragged on for a year.
The father remains intransigent: his daughter will not marry a sailor.
My brother is intransigent about the thermostat and will not move it one degree.

confused.note: Intransigent means refusing to compromise; an intransitive verb takes no object.

questions.passage: Negotiators had hoped that the union would accept a smaller raise in exchange for better health coverage. Its leaders proved ______, repeating that they would sign nothing short of their original demand.
questions.explanation: Refusing anything short of the original demand is refusing to compromise.

distractors.why: Amenable means willing to agree, which the leaders were not.
Diffident means lacking confidence, but the leaders were firm.
Fickle means changing one's mind often, but they never budged.

partsNote: not coming across to an agreement

definition: shy and lacking confidence in one's own ability

examples.text: The diffident clerk rehearses his request three times before knocking.
Diffident in public, the queen left speeches to her ministers.
She gave a diffident wave, unsure whether I would remember her.

confused.note: Diffident means shy; it has nothing to do with being different.

questions.passage: Although her research was the most original in the department, the young physicist was ______ about it. She spoke so quietly at seminars that listeners had to lean forward, and she rarely volunteered her results.
questions.explanation: Speaking quietly and holding back results shows shyness and low confidence.

distractors.why: Presumptuous means overly bold, the opposite of her manner.
Adamant means firmly insistent, which she was not.
Skeptical means doubtful of a claim; the passage describes shyness about presenting her work.

definition: very great, deep, or showing great knowledge and insight

examples.text: The invention of the microscope had a profound effect on medicine.
The simple fable carries a profound lesson about pride.
Moving to a new country at twelve had a profound influence on how I see the world.

confused.note: Profound means deep; profuse means plentiful, as in "profuse apologies."

questions.passage: The printing press did more than make books cheaper. Its effects were ______: within a century it had changed how people worshiped, how governments ruled, and how scientists shared discoveries.
questions.explanation: Changing religion, government, and science is a very deep effect.

distractors.why: Superficial means shallow, the opposite of such sweeping change.
Transient means short-lived, but these changes lasted.
Perfunctory means done without care, which does not describe effects.

definition: able to be believed or trusted

examples.text: No credible study has ever linked the vaccine to the illness.
The spy's report seemed credible because it matched what scouts had seen.
"The bus was late" is a credible excuse; "aliens took my homework" is not.

confused.note: Credible describes a believable claim or source; credulous describes a person who believes too easily.

questions.passage: The newspaper will not print an accusation unless it comes from a ______ source. Reporters must show that the person was in a position to know the facts and has no record of misleading the press.
questions.explanation: A source who knows the facts and has not misled before can be believed.

distractors.why: Credulous describes someone who believes too easily, not a source worth believing.
Anonymous means unnamed; the standard described is about trustworthiness.
Spurious means false, which is what the paper wants to avoid.

definition: logical, well organized, and easy to understand

examples.text: The data fit together into a coherent picture of how the virus spreads.
The diary's scattered entries never form a coherent story.
I was too sleepy at 6 a.m. to give a coherent answer.

confused.note: Coherent means logically connected and understandable; cohesive means sticking together as a united group.

questions.passage: The first draft of the report jumped from topic to topic with no clear thread. After the editor rearranged its sections so that each built on the one before, the argument finally became ______.
questions.explanation: Sections that build on one another make an argument logical and easy to follow.

distractors.why: Disjointed means disconnected, which describes the first draft.
Equivocal means deliberately unclear, which reordering sections would not produce.
Exorbitant means unreasonably expensive, which does not apply to an argument.
